tagline.text: Camiguin's tallest waterfall at about 76 m, with an orchid-fringed pool

location.label: Location
location.text: Outskirts of Mambajao, Camiguin (about 5 km southeast of the town center, at the foot of Mount Timpoong)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱75–400 (entrance fee, round-trip transport from town and snacks, per person)

children.text: Katibawasan Falls is Camiguin's tallest waterfall, dropping about 76 m, and lies a 10–15 minute ride from Mambajao town. A paved staircase from the parking area leads down to a plunge pool ringed by orchids and ferns.

Katibawasan Falls sits at the foot of Mount Timpoong, about 5 km southeast of Mambajao, the capital of Camiguin Island in the southern Philippines. Sources give slightly different heights of 70 m, about 76 m and 80 m, but most guides describe it as the tallest waterfall on the island. English Wikipedia says it drops about 250 feet (76 m) into a pool surrounded by orchids and ferns.

Camiguin is a single volcanic island packed with several volcanoes, so waterfalls, hot springs, a sunken cemetery and a white sandbar all sit within one loop around the island. Of these, Katibawasan is the waterfall closest to Mambajao, where the airport and port are. A paved road runs all the way to the parking lot at the entrance, and the path from the entrance down to the pool is also a paved staircase, so no hiking gear and no forest trek are needed.

At the foot of the falls is a shallow pool that has been partly shaped by people. It is not big enough for real swimming, but it is plenty for wading, standing in the spray and cooling off. Go early and you can take photos in peace; around midday tour groups crowd in.

It works well at the start or end of an island loop that includes White Island, the sunken cemetery or a view of the old volcano. Think of it as a stop of a little over an hour within a half-day plan rather than a place to spend long. The national road that circles the coast is about
64 km

long, so Camiguin is small enough to ride around by motorbike in a day. Seeing the falls at one end of Mambajao and then heading out along the coast road lets you fit in other sights the same day, which suits short itineraries. The water comes down from the highlands around Mount Timpoong (the highest peak in the area at about
, part of the Mount Mambajao protected area), and English Wikipedia notes that this area was declared an ASEAN Heritage Park in 2015.
Sources disagree on the drop, from 70 to 80 m, but many give about 76 m (250 feet). A single ribbon of water falls down the rock face, and you can take in the whole sight at a glance.

Pass the ticket booth near the parking lot and follow the zigzag staircase down. Guides count roughly 100–200 steps, and many describe them as not steep, so children and older visitors can go down at an easy pace. You have to climb back up, though, so take care not to slip while wet.

The pool below the falls is clear and cold, ideal for cooling off in the tropical midday heat. Many reviews say it is too small for swimming, so plan on wading and a quick dip. The bottom is mostly rock.

Ferns and orchids grow around the falls thanks to the damp air. Take a moment to enjoy the cool air created by the water coming down from the Mount Timpoong side. The path is through humid forest, so mosquitoes and insects are possible; long sleeves or repellent help.

blocks.title: A snack shop at the gate

children.text: A small shop outside the entrance sells snacks, drinks and local treats. One guide recommends kiping, a Camiguin snack of flat cassava wafer brushed with molasses. Stock varies from day to day.

blocks.title: Easy to fit into an island loop

children.text: It is close to Mambajao town and the airport, so it fits well on the afternoon you arrive or the morning you leave. One guide puts the drive from Mambajao at about
10 minutes
and another at
15 minutes

items.title: Half-day plan
items.subtitle: See the falls first, then head to town and the coast

children.text: Leave your Mambajao lodging by motorbike or tricycle. The falls are about
10–15 minutes
from town along an inland road, and the parking lot at the end of the road is the terminus.
Pay the entrance fee at the ticket booth and go in. Guides list the fee anywhere from ₱50 to ₱75, so confirm on site.
Walk down the stairs to the pool. It is better to take photos before the sun gets strong. Dip your feet and cool off lightly.
Climb back up, buy a snack at the shop by the gate and return to the parking lot.
Head back to town for lunch, then move on to White Island or the sunken cemetery in the afternoon.

items.title: Full-day island loop
items.subtitle: The falls plus a lap of the island

children.text: Start with Katibawasan Falls.
Head back toward Mambajao and add another waterfall or hot spring on Camiguin. Guides say Tuasan Falls is farther away.
Have lunch in town or at a seaside restaurant.
Move on to the sunken cemetery or the Guiob church ruins. See their own entries for details.
End the day watching the sunset from the coast road. One guide describes the Tongatok cliff area as a sunset spot.
Travel times assume a motorbike and vary with road conditions.
This research did not confirm any direct flight from Manila to Camiguin. Check the airlines' latest schedules.
The most common route is to fly from Manila to Cagayan de Oro (Laguindingan Airport, CGY), then continue to Camiguin by road and boat.
According to one guide, take a shuttle from Laguindingan Airport to the Agora Bus Terminal in Cagayan de Oro, then an eastbound bus toward the port of Balingoan, which takes about
2 hours
. The boat from Balingoan to Benoni port takes
1 to 1.5 hours
depending on the operator and weather, and departures from Balingoan reportedly run between
and
by operator (as listed in June 2026; schedules change without notice, so confirm locally).

From Mactan-Cebu International Airport, Cebu Pacific's affiliate Cebgo is described as flying to Camiguin Airport about once a day (roughly 9 flights a week). Flights change by season and date, so check before booking.
Port and flight times and whether services run change often.
The falls are about
5 km
from Mambajao town. One guide says it takes about
15 minutes
by motorbike from Mambajao.
Guides say there is no regular public transport to the falls. Take a tricycle or a habal-habal (motorbike taxi) and ask the driver to wait and bring you back.
Guides list scooter rental at about
a day (fuel and insurance terms vary by shop).
The road climbs gently inland from town and ends at the falls' parking lot. Signs are said to make it easy to find.

Many guides say the dry season, November to April, is easy for planning, with low humidity and little rain. Others say the water is fullest right after heavy rain. Check the weather forecast when choosing your dates.

After heavy rain the falls are more impressive, but the steps and ground are slippery and the water can turn murky. Weather varies from year to year, so check the forecast before you set out.

Lodging in the Mambajao town and airport area is closest to the falls. One guide recommends places with a pool near the airport and port. Beachside stays are convenient for sunsets and for connecting the island loop, but are a little farther from the falls.
There is no restaurant at the falls, only a small shop outside the entrance. Have lunch in Mambajao town and bring your own water and snacks. One guide recommends kiping from the shop at the gate.

You can eat fairly cheaply at local restaurants and the market in Mambajao town. Camiguin is also known for the Lanzones Festival, held around the third weekend of October, when rooms and boat seats fill up early, so check ahead. If you want to fit the falls, hot springs and coast into one day, basing yourself between Mambajao and Catarman cuts travel time.
Bring swimwear, a change of dry clothes and a waterproof bag. Restrooms and showers are reported just inside the entrance.
Reviews say the restroom lighting can be dim, so carry your phone's flashlight.
The steps can be slippery when wet. Wear grippy sandals or water shoes rather than flip-flops.
Carry enough cash. Entrance fees, snacks and transport are mainly paid in cash.
If you rent a scooter, check license requirements and local rules, and always wear a helmet.
Guides warn that standing right under the falling water is dangerous. Do not go directly beneath the falls.
Between

it is crowded and the glare on the rocks is harsh. Shoot photos in the morning or late afternoon.
The area directly below the falls is dangerous because of falling water and slippery rock, so keep away, and after rain the water level can rise suddenly, so follow safety signs.
Entrance fees, opening hours and step counts differ by source, so confirm them on site.
On heavy-rain days or during typhoons the road and steps get slippery and access may be restricted.
The pool is not big enough for real swimming and the bottom is rock. Children must stay with an adult at all times.
Keep valuables in a waterproof bag and do not leave them unattended on the rocks.
The scooter road can mix unpaved stretches with climbs, so slow down.
A sandbar off the north coast, described by one guide as a sunrise spot. Some descriptions place it about
5 km
west of Mambajao.

blocks.title: Sunken Cemetery and Guiob Church Ruins

children.text: The cemetery and church ruins of an old village sunk by a volcanic eruption. Described as a snorkeling spot.
